author: sonnet
final_message:
All three versions (`rust/src/main.rs`, `plain.py`, `fast.py`) match the expected output byte for byte on s1, s2 and s3.

I also built a 30,000-line stress input with escaped account names, channels and tags (such as `"\u0074est"`), surrogate pairs, shuffled keys, odd whitespace, nested decoy `account`, `type`, `tags` and `channel` keys, and tied account sums. All three versions produced identical output on it. I checked them against each other only, since there was no independent reference output.

**Algorithm:** All three read the file in chunks, parse each transaction and skip `void` and `test`-tagged ones. Amounts become integer hundredths, then `usd = h*rate // 1000000`, negated for `debit`. Per-channel (count, net) and per-account sums are accumulated. At the end, channels sort by name and the top 10 accounts sort by sum descending, then ID.

**Rust:**
- It uses a hand-written single-pass parser over 4 MB chunks, so memory stays flat.
- It reads only the keys it needs and skips every other value without building anything.
- Strings stay as slices of the buffer, and are decoded (including `\uXXXX` and surrogate pairs) only when they contain a backslash.
- Amounts are parsed straight from bytes, and the maps use a custom Fx-style hasher.
- Release profile is `lto = true`, `codegen-units = 1`, `panic = "abort"`.
- A synthetic 380 MB file (s3 repeated 20 times) took about 0.85–3 s. The machine was noisy, so treat that as a range.

**`plain.py`:**
- It reads 4 MB binary chunks and parses each chunk with a single `json.loads` call, so the C parser handles all the escapes and decoys. This is much cheaper than one call per line.
- Garbage collection is disabled, which cut the 380 MB run from about 13–19 s to about 7–10 s.
- The aggregation loop uses dict `.get` and a precomputed sign table.

**`fast.py`:**
- It uses the same chunked `json.loads` with GC disabled.
- Fields are pulled out with `map(itemgetter(...))`, and the `void`/`test` filter is a NumPy boolean mask plus `itertools.compress`.
- Amount strings are turned into hundredths with vectorised digit arithmetic.
- Accounts and channels get dense ids through a dict, and sums use `np.add.at` on int64 so they stay exact.
- On the 380 MB synthetic file it was about as fast as `plain.py`, or slightly slower (roughly 11–13 s against 7–10 s), because JSON parsing dominates and NumPy's import costs about 0.2 s.

Python timings varied a lot between runs because other programs were using the machine.

request.prompt:
You are writing three versions of the same program, one in Rust and two in Python, for a comparison of how
fast and how memory-hungry each version is.

The task is described in SPEC.md in this folder. The folder samples/ holds example inputs (`*.in`), each with
the exact expected output (`*.out`).

Write these three files:

1. `rust/src/main.rs`: Rust, compiled with rustc 1.99 (edition 2024). The Cargo project in `rust/` is set
   up. The only crates you may use are serde (with derive), serde_json, regex and rayon. They are already
   listed in `rust/Cargo.toml` and vendored, so build offline with `cargo build --release --offline` inside
   `rust/`. Do not add other dependencies. You may change the `[profile.release]` settings in
   `rust/Cargo.toml`.
2. `plain.py`: Python 3.13, standard library only.
3. `fast.py`: Python 3.13, standard library plus NumPy 2.2.

Each program is run with the path of one input file as its argument (SPEC.md says if a task takes more
arguments). It reads that file and writes the answer to standard output exactly as SPEC.md describes. The
Python versions are run as `C:\Python313\python.exe plain.py INPUT_PATH` and
`C:\Python313\python.exe fast.py INPUT_PATH`, and the Rust version as the release binary
`rust/target/release/solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.

Your goals, in order:

1. Every version must print the correct output for any valid input as SPEC.md defines it, not only for the
   samples.
2. Make each version as fast as you can. Write each one the way a skilled developer in that language would
   write fast code, using that language's own strengths.

Use a single thread and a single process unless SPEC.md says otherwise. Do not precompute or embed answers,
start other programs, or read any file other than the input.

The programs will be run on Windows 11 on a 16-core laptop, on larger inputs of the same kind; SPEC.md gives
the benchmark size. Test all three versions against every sample before you finish. Work only inside this
folder, and take at most about 45 minutes. Other programs run on this machine at the same time:
never stop a process you did not start yourself, so do not kill processes by name (for example
`taskkill /IM python.exe` or `Stop-Process -Name python`); stop only your own processes, by process ID.

When you are done, reply with a short summary: the algorithm, the main choices you made for speed in each
version, and which samples each version passes.
